name: The Usera Route
tagline: 7 riddles from Metro Usera to the “broken church” in Pradolongo

place.name: Metro Usera, Calle de Amparo Usera

stops.riddle: A colonel’s family still walks these streets, at least by name.
stops.whereHint: Come up at Usera metro station (line 6), exit Calle de Amparo Usera.
stops.look: Read the street sign by the metro exit
stops.question: Who is Calle de Amparo Usera named after?
options: A member of the Usera family
stops.answer: A member of the Usera family
stops.hint: Look at the surname: it’s the name of the whole district.

lesson.title: A neighbourhood named after a family

image.alt: The entrance to Usera metro station, with the red Metro sign

lesson.subtitle: How a farmer’s fields became a barrio, and why its streets have first names
lesson.recap: Usera is named after a colonel, and its streets after his family

numbers.label: the fields start being sold as plots

story.text: This land belonged to a farmer from Villaverde known as “Tío Sordillo”. His daughter, Carmen del Río, married Colonel Marcelo Usera, a soldier and businessman who decided houses would pay better than crops.
Between 1925 and 1930 the fields were divided into plots and sold. Working families from all over Spain built their homes here.

The colonel’s administrator drew the street plan and named the streets after the Usera family, their staff and some neighbours. That’s why you walk along Amparo Usera, Gabriel Usera and Isabelita Usera.

timeline.text: The Usera fields start being sold as building plots
Villaverde, which owned most of this land, becomes part of Madrid
Families arrive from rural Spain and the barrio grows fast
Usera becomes its own district of Madrid
Usera becomes Madrid’s Chinatown

context.title: Madrid grew by swallowing villages
context.text: Many districts you know today were separate towns until the 1940s and 1950s: Carabanchel, Vallecas, Villaverde. As Madrid grew, it absorbed them, and their fields became neighbourhoods like this one.

lookCloser.title: Street signs.
lookCloser.text: Madrid’s blue-and-white tiled street signs often have a small picture. Look for the ones around the station.

lookCloser.title: Shop signs.
lookCloser.text: Count the shop signs in Chinese characters you can see from here. There will be more soon.

lesson.think: If you could name the street where you live after someone in your family, who would it be?

check.question: What was this land before the 1920s?

place.name: Colonia Moscardó sundials, Calle de Gumersindo de Azcárate

stops.riddle: Here, the walls tell the time, but only when the sky is clear.
stops.whereHint: Corner of Calle de Gumersindo de Azcárate and Calle de Gabriel Usera, two blocks west of the metro.
stops.look: Look up at the walls and passages around you
stops.question: How many sundials are hidden in these streets?
stops.hint: More than a dozen, fewer than twenty.

lesson.title: The 17 sundials of Moscardó
lesson.subtitle: An open-air clock museum painted on the walls of a 1920s housing estate
lesson.recap: 17 sundials designed by an artist and a mathematician

story.text: In the 1980s the designer Alberto Corazón and the mathematician Juan José Caurcel teamed up to put sundials on these walls: one brought the art, the other the maths of shadows (called gnomonics).
There are 17 of them on the façades and passages of Calle de Gumersindo de Azcárate, Doctor Sanchís Banús and Ramón de Madariaga. Each one is different.

These houses were planned around 1928 as the “Salud y Ahorro” (Health and Savings) estate, one of Madrid’s early housing projects for working families. After the Civil War it was renamed after General Moscardó, and the name stuck.

timeline.text: Building starts on the Salud y Ahorro estate
Renamed Colonia Moscardó
Alberto Corazón and Juan José Caurcel design the sundials
The sundials are restored

context.title: Why the sundial disagrees with your phone
context.text: A sundial shows solar time: noon is when the sun is highest. Spain uses Central European Time, even though Madrid is west of Greenwich, so the sun is highest here around 1:15 pm in winter and 2:15 pm in summer. If a dial says 12 and your phone says 2, both are right.

lookCloser.title: The pointer.
lookCloser.text: Find a dial’s metal rod (the gnomon). It is tilted to point at the North Star, so it is parallel to the Earth’s axis.

lookCloser.title: Hunt them all.
lookCloser.text: Walk the nearby passages and count how many dials you can find. Some are easy to miss.

lesson.think: If clocks had never been invented, how would you agree with a friend on what time to meet?

check.question: When is the sun highest in Madrid in summer, by the clock?

place.name: Biblioteca Pública José Hierro, Avenida de Rafaela Ybarra 43

stops.riddle: A poet’s house of books stands up straight instead of lying down.
stops.look: Step back and look at the whole building
stops.question: What is unusual about this library?

lesson.title: Biblioteca José Hierro

image.alt: The José Hierro library: a tall block clad in grey panels

lesson.subtitle: A library that grows upwards, named after a poet
lesson.recap: A tower of books named after a Cervantes Prize poet

numbers.label: José Hierro wins the Cervantes Prize

story.text: Instead of a wide, low building, the architects Iñaki Ábalos and Juan Herreros stacked the library into a slim tower in the middle of a residential neighbourhood. It opened on 9 October 2003.

A Madrid-born poet (1922–2002) who was jailed for years after the Civil War and later became one of Spain’s best-loved writers. In 1998 he won the Cervantes Prize, the top award for writers in Spanish.
Each level has a different use, from children’s books to quiet reading rooms. It’s free, like every public library in Madrid.

timeline.text: José Hierro is born in Madrid
He wins the Cervantes Prize
José Hierro dies in Madrid
The library opens in Usera

context.title: Why build a library as a tower?
context.text: Space is scarce in a dense neighbourhood. A tower leaves room for a square at its foot and becomes a landmark you can see from far away, a bit like a bell tower for books.

lookCloser.title: The walls.
lookCloser.text: Look at the outside skin of the building. Can you see what’s happening inside from the street?

lookCloser.title: The name.
lookCloser.text: Find José Hierro’s name on the building.

lesson.think: Would you rather read in a cosy basement or at the top of a tower? Why?

check.question: Which prize did José Hierro win in 1998?

stops.riddle: Two dragons and a Madrid local guard the newest gate in the city.
stops.whereHint: Plaza del Hidrógeno, on Calle de Dolores Barranco.
stops.look: Look at the figures on the arch
stops.question: Which animal from Madrid’s coat of arms stands with the two dragons?
stops.hint: You might have met it on the Puerta del Sol, eating from a tree.

lesson.title: Madrid’s first Chinese arch

image.alt: A red lion-dance costume at the Chinese New Year parade in Usera

lesson.subtitle: A gateway where two dragons meet the Madrid bear
lesson.recap: A paifang by Okuda: two dragons for China, a bear for Madrid

story.text: A paifang is a traditional Chinese gateway. Chinatowns from London to San Francisco have one at their entrance. This is the first in Madrid, unveiled in October 2026.

The artist Okuda San Miguel, known for his multicoloured geometric style, surrounded it with two dragons, a symbol of China, and a bear, the symbol of Madrid. It was made together with the district and the local Chinese community.
You’re on Calle de Dolores Barranco, the heart of Usera’s Chinatown, with its supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants. A second arch is planned on Calle de los Evangelios.

timeline.text: Usera becomes Madrid’s Chinatown
The city plans two Chinese arches for Usera
Okuda’s arch is unveiled in the Plaza del Hidrógeno

context.title: Where is everyone from?
context.text: Usera has the largest Chinese community in Spain. Many families come from Zhejiang province in eastern China, especially the county of Qingtian, known for sending people all over Europe.

lookCloser.title: The colours.
lookCloser.text: Okuda uses rainbow triangles and geometric faces. Find his style on the dragons.

lookCloser.title: The writing.
lookCloser.text: Look for Chinese characters on the arch and on the shop signs around you.

lesson.think: If your town made a gate to welcome visitors, what two symbols would you put on it?

check.question: What does the dragon stand for on the arch?

place.name: Panda statue, Calle de la Pilarica with Calle de Julio Merino

stops.riddle: A black-and-white treasure from far away sits still at a crossroads.
stops.whereHint: Follow Dolores Barranco east, then find the corner of Calle de la Pilarica and Calle de Julio Merino.
stops.question: What is the panda made of?
stops.hint: It’s a stone, cold and smooth.

lesson.title: The Usera panda
lesson.subtitle: Half a tonne of marble at a neighbourhood crossroads
lesson.recap: A marble panda, a gift and a symbol of friendship

story.text: In China the giant panda is called a national treasure, and pandas have long been sent abroad as gifts of friendship.
This marble panda on a granite base was presented in autumn 2022 as a gift from the district’s Chinese community, a symbol of living together.
Some neighbours pointed out that the messages on the pedestal were written in English and Chinese, but not in Spanish. Public art often starts conversations like that.

timeline.text: Madrid Zoo receives its first giant pandas, a gift from China
The marble panda arrives in Usera
The first Chinese arch opens a few streets away

context.title: Chinese New Year in Usera
context.text: Every year, around late January or February, Usera holds Madrid’s big Chinese New Year parade, with dragons, lions and drums. Hundreds of thousands of people come to watch.

lookCloser.title: The pedestal.
lookCloser.text: Read the messages on the base. Which languages can you spot?

lookCloser.title: The paws.
lookCloser.text: Is the panda eating, sitting or playing?

lesson.think: Should messages on public statues be written in every language spoken in the neighbourhood?

check.question: Why are pandas often given as gifts by China?

stops.riddle: The neighbours drew this green space themselves. Find its garden of geometric beds.
stops.whereHint: Parque de Pradolongo: the botanical garden is next to the lake.
stops.look: Look for the shrub with small red berries
stops.question: Which tree from Madrid’s coat of arms grows in this garden?

lesson.title: Parque de Pradolongo

image.alt: Paths and geometric beds in the Pradolongo botanical garden

lesson.subtitle: The park the neighbours designed
lesson.recap: A huge park shaped by its neighbours, opened in 1983

numbers.label: species of trees and shrubs in the garden

story.text: Pradolongo opened in 1983 under Madrid’s mayor Enrique Tierno Galván. It is often called the first “democratic” park because it was designed around what the people who would use it asked for.
The botanical garden next to the lake has 30 geometric flower beds arranged around seven small squares, with around 180 species of trees and shrubs: pines, cedars, oaks, olives and palms.
Among the native plants is the madroño, the strawberry tree from Madrid’s coat of arms, along with rosemary, thyme and lavender.

timeline.text: The botanical garden is laid out
The park opens under mayor Tierno Galván
The lake area is restored
The Chinese New Year parade moves to the park

context.title: What makes a park “democratic”?
context.text: After 1975 Spain returned to democracy, and the first elected city councils took office in 1979. Neighbourhood associations, especially in the south of Madrid, fought for parks, schools and clinics, and often helped decide what they would be like.

lookCloser.title: The lake.
lookCloser.text: Look for goals hanging above the water: they’re for kayak polo, a mix of canoeing and water polo.

lookCloser.title: Smell test.
lookCloser.text: Rub a leaf of rosemary or thyme between your fingers (without picking it).

lesson.think: If you could design a park for your neighbourhood, what’s the first thing you would put in it?

check.question: Who helped decide how the park would look?

place.name: Maris Stella, the “broken church”, Calle del Doctor Tolosa Latour 16

stops.riddle: They called me the broken church. A bird still keeps watch on my roof.
stops.whereHint: East edge of Pradolongo park, on Calle del Doctor Tolosa Latour.
stops.look: Look at the very top of the dome
stops.question: What stands on top of the dome?
stops.hint: Locals also call it “the church of the …”, after a farmyard bird.

lesson.title: Maris Stella, the “broken church”

image.alt: The Maris Stella chapel and its dome behind a railing, with the sign of the environmental centre

lesson.subtitle: From a wartime ruin to a school, and now a centre for nature
lesson.recap: The “broken church” with a rooster on its dome

story.text: Maris Stella is Latin for “Star of the Sea”, an old name for the Virgin Mary. Nobody knows exactly when this brick chapel was built, but it dates from the early 20th century.
It was badly damaged in the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), so locals called it “la iglesia rota”. Others call it “the church of the rooster”, after the bird on its dome.

Families arriving from Castilla-La Mancha and Extremadura built homes nearby by hand, the start of the Orcasitas neighbourhood. For years this was the only building fit for a school, and children learned to read here.

timeline.text: The chapel is built
The Civil War begins; the church is badly damaged
It is used as a church and a school
It is the Maris Stella environmental and cultural centre

context.title: Orcasitas: the neighbours who stayed
context.text: In the 1970s the people of Orcasitas organised to replace their shacks with proper homes in the same place, instead of being moved away. Their neighbourhood association became one of the most famous in Spain.

lookCloser.title: The dome.
lookCloser.text: Count the sides of the dome. It’s an unusual shape for a church.

lookCloser.title: The bricks.
lookCloser.text: Look for patches where the brickwork changes: the scars of repairs.

lesson.think: Is it better to rebuild an old building as it was, or give it a new life with a new use?
